headline: How Sperm Whales Blow Bubbles to Stay Asleep
meta_description: Scientists discover sperm whales release bubbles while sleeping underwater to prevent themselves from floating to the surface like corks.
summary_short: Researchers tracked 42 sperm whales off Norway and found they deliberately blow bubbles while napping underwater—a clever trick to stay submerged and rest.
body:
For decades, scientists puzzled over how sperm whales could possibly sleep underwater without bobbing to the surface. The answer, revealed by researchers from the University of St. Andrews in Scotland and the University of Neuchâtel in Switzerland, is elegantly simple: they blow bubbles. The ocean giants, which doze in brief 10- to 15-minute stretches with their heads pointing upward, face a buoyancy problem. Their massive heads—comprising nearly a third of their bodies—are filled with oil, wax, and air, materials that naturally float. By deliberately releasing bubbles from their blowholes, the whales reduce their buoyancy enough to stay down. The discovery emerged from a high-tech field study conducted off the Lofoten Islands, Norway, where researchers attached recording devices to 42 sperm whales. These instruments tracked bubble release, water depth, and head orientation as the whales slept.

The data revealed that resting depth dramatically shapes bubble behavior. Whales dozing near the surface released bubbles roughly 11 times during each nap, actively fighting their natural tendency to rise. Those drifting upward from deep dives exceeding 200 meters, by contrast, blew bubbles only three or four times—the water pressure already compressing the air in their lungs, making them less buoyant. The findings, published in the Journal of Experimental Biology, suggest the whales have adapted a sophisticated sleep strategy to different ocean zones.

What remains unclear is whether sperm whales consciously control this bubble release or operate on some automatic reflex—or indeed, whether they sleep as we do at all. Study lead author Noémie Freymond notes that sperm whales may sleep like dolphins, keeping half their brain alert while the other rests. Still, whatever the mechanism, these deep-diving marine mammals have engineered a remarkably creative solution to a fundamental problem: staying soundly asleep in an environment built to push them toward the surface.
quick_facts: Scientists tracked 42 sperm whales off Norway's Lofoten Islands
Whales near surface blow bubbles ~11 times per 10-15 minute nap
Sperm whale heads make up one-third of body, filled with floating materials
Research published in Journal of Experimental Biology by Scottish and Swiss universities
